title: GATE Mathematics Topic Test: Topology — Set 1
titleEn: GATE Mathematics Topic Test: Topology — Set 1
titleHi: गेट गणित टॉपिक टेस्ट: संस्थिति विज्ञान (टोपोलॉजी) — सेट 1

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be an infinite set endowed with the cofinite topology $\tau_{\text{cf}}$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
optionsEn: Only finite subsets of $X$ are compact
$X$ is compact, but proper infinite subsets of $X$ are not compact
questions.explanationEn: Let $A \subseteq X$ be any nonempty subset and $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $A$ in $(X, \tau_{\text{cf}})$. Pick one $U_{\alpha_0}$ meeting $A$. Since $X \setminus U_{\alpha_0}$ is finite, $A \setminus U_{\alpha_0}$ contains at most finitely many points, each covered by one set from $\{U_\alpha\}$. This yields a finite subcover, so every subset of $X$ is compact.

questions.questionTextEn: Urysohn's Lemma states that a $T_1$ topological space $X$ is normal if and only if for every pair of disjoint closed subsets $A, B \subseteq X$, there exists a continuous function $f : X \to [0, 1]$ such that:
optionsEn: $f(x) = 0$ for all $x \in A$ and $f(x) = 1$ for all $x \in B$
questions.explanationEn: Urysohn's Lemma guarantees a continuous function $f : X \to [0, 1]$ with $f(A) \subseteq \{0\}$ and $f(B) \subseteq \{1\}$ (and conversely, such functions yield disjoint open neighborhoods $f^{-1}([0, 1/3))$ and $f^{-1}((2/3, 1])$ of $A$ and $B$). Requiring $f^{-1}(\{0\}) = A$ strictly is the stronger condition of perfect normality, not general normality.

questions.questionTextEn: On $\mathbb{R}$, let $\tau_u$ be the usual topology, $\tau_l$ be the lower limit topology generated by $\{[a, b) : a < b\}$, and $\tau_K$ be the $K$-topology generated by usual open intervals together with sets of the form $(a, b) \setminus K$ where $K = \{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. Which of the following inclusion relations is TRUE?
questions.explanationEn: Both $\tau_l$ and $\tau_K$ are strictly finer than $\tau_u$. The set $[1, 2)$ is open in $\tau_l$ but not in $\tau_K$ (no basis element of $\tau_K$ containing $1$ lies inside $[1, 2)$). Conversely, $(-1, 1) \setminus K$ is open in $\tau_K$ and contains $0$, but every $\tau_l$-basis element $[0, b)$ contains $1/n \in K$ for large $n$, so $(-1, 1) \setminus K \notin \tau_l$. Thus $\tau_l$ and $\tau_K$ are incomparable.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about the Sorgenfrey line $\mathbb{R}_l$ is FALSE?
questions.explanationEn: At each $x \in \mathbb{R}_l$, $\{[x, x + 1/n) : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ is a countable local basis (first countable), $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable and dense (separable), and $\mathbb{R}_l$ is Lindel\"of. However, any basis $\mathcal{B}$ for $\mathbb{R}_l$ must contain, for each $x \in \mathbb{R}$, a set $B_x \in \mathcal{B}$ with $\inf B_x = x$, so $B_x \neq B_y$ for $x \neq y$. Hence $\mathcal{B}$ is uncountable, and $\mathbb{R}_l$ is not second countable.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the diagonal map $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^\omega$ defined by $f(t) = (t, t, t, \dots)$, where $\mathbb{R}^\omega$ is the countably infinite product of $\mathbb{R}$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
optionsEn: $f$ is continuous in both the product topology and the box topology on $\mathbb{R}^\omega$
$f$ is continuous in the product topology on $\mathbb{R}^\omega$, but not in the box topology
$f$ is continuous in the box topology on $\mathbb{R}^\omega$, but not in the product topology
$f$ is discontinuous in both the product topology and the box topology on $\mathbb{R}^\omega$
questions.explanationEn: Each coordinate function $f_n(t) = t$ is continuous, so $f$ is continuous in the product topology. In the box topology, consider the open neighborhood $B = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1/n, 1/n)$ of $f(0) = (0, 0, \dots)$. Then $f^{-1}(B) = \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1/n, 1/n) = \{0\}$, which is not open in $\mathbb{R}$. Hence $f$ is not continuous in the box topology.

questions.questionTextEn: Consider the ordered square $I_o^2 = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ with the dictionary order topology. Which of the following properties does $I_o^2$ satisfy?
questions.explanationEn: $I_o^2$ is a linear continuum with a least element $(0, 0)$ and greatest element $(1, 1)$, so it is compact (A) and connected (B). However, it is not path-connected (C is false: a continuous path from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$ would cover all uncountably many disjoint open vertical segments $\{x\} \times (0, 1)$, contradicting the separability/second countability of $[0, 1]$) and not second countable (D is false, since $\{\{x\} \times (0, 1) : x \in [0, 1]\}$ is an uncountable family of pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $p : X \to Y$ be a continuous surjective map between topological spaces. Which of the following conditions is/are SUFFICIENT to ensure that $p$ is a quotient map?
optionsEn: There exists a continuous map $s : Y \to X$ such that $p \circ s = \operatorname{id}_Y$
questions.explanationEn: Every continuous surjective open map (A) or closed map (B) is a quotient map. If $X$ is compact and $Y$ is Hausdorff (C), then $p$ is automatically a closed map and hence a quotient map. If $p$ has a continuous section $s$ with $p \circ s = \operatorname{id}_Y$ (D), then whenever $p^{-1}(U)$ is open in $X$, $U = s^{-1}(p^{-1}(U))$ is open in $Y$, so $p$ is a quotient map.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following topological spaces are normal ($T_4$)?
questions.explanationEn: Every metric space is normal (A), every compact Hausdorff space is normal (B), and every regular Lindel\"of space is normal (C, a classic theorem of Tychonoff). Not every Hausdorff space is normal (D is false; e.g., $\mathbb{R}_K$ is Hausdorff but not even regular).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ be equipped with the discrete topology and $Y = \{0, 1\}$ be equipped with the discrete topology. How many continuous functions $f : X \to Y$ exist?
questions.explanationEn: Since $X$ has the discrete topology, every function $f : X \to Y$ is continuous. There are $|Y|^{|X|} = 2^4 = 16$ such functions.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ have the topology $\tau$ generated by the subbasis $\mathcal{S} = \{\{1, 2, 3\}, \{2, 3, 4\}, \{4, 5\}\}$. What is the total number of open sets in $\tau$?
questions.explanationEn: Taking all finite intersections of elements in $\mathcal{S}$ gives the basis $\mathcal{B} = \{\emptyset, \{4\}, \{2, 3\}, \{4, 5\}, \{1, 2, 3\}, \{2, 3, 4\}, X\}$. Forming all arbitrary unions of sets in $\mathcal{B}$ yields the $9$ distinct open sets: $\emptyset$, $\{4\}$, $\{2, 3\}$, $\{4, 5\}$, $\{1, 2, 3\}$, $\{2, 3, 4\}$, $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, $\{2, 3, 4, 5\}$, and $X$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be the comb space defined by $C = ([0, 1] \times \{0\}) \cup (\{0\} \times [0, 1]) \cup \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} (\{1/n\} \times [0, 1])$, and let $C^* = C \setminus (\{0\} \times (0, 1))$ be the deleted comb space (so $(0, 1) \in C^*$ and $(0, 0) \in C^*$). Which of the following is TRUE about $C^*$?
questions.explanationEn: The subset $C_0 = ([0, 1] \times \{0\}) \cup \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} (\{1/n\} \times [0, 1])$ is path-connected, and $C_0 \subseteq C^* \subseteq \overline{C_0} = C$, so $C^*$ is connected. However, any continuous path in $C^*$ starting at $(0, 1)$ must stay within a small neighborhood of $(0, 1)$ whose vertical segments are disconnected from each other in that neighborhood, forcing the path to be constant at $(0, 1)$. Hence $C^*$ is not path-connected (and not closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$, so not compact).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a connected normal space containing at least two distinct points. What is the minimum possible cardinality of $X$?
questions.explanationEn: Let $x \neq y$ be two points in the connected normal ($T_4$) space $X$. Since singletons are closed in a $T_4$ space, Urysohn's Lemma provides a continuous function $f : X \to [0, 1]$ with $f(x) = 0$ and $f(y) = 1$. Since $X$ is connected, $f(X)$ is a connected subset of $[0, 1]$ containing $0$ and $1$, so $f(X) = [0, 1]$. Thus $|X| \ge |[0, 1]| = \mathfrak{c}$ (and $X = [0, 1]$ achieves this minimum).

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X$ be a normal space and $A \subseteq X$ be a closed subset. Let $S^1 = \{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x^2 + y^2 = 1\}$ and $D^2 = \{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x^2 + y^2 \le 1\}$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
optionsEn: Every continuous map $f : A \to S^1$ extends to a continuous map $F : X \to S^1$
Every continuous map $f : A \to D^2$ extends to a continuous map $F : X \to D^2$
Neither $S^1$-valued nor $D^2$-valued continuous maps on $A$ necessarily extend to $X$
Every continuous map $f : A \to \{0, 1\}$ extends to a continuous map $F : X \to \{0, 1\}$
questions.explanationEn: The closed disk $D^2$ is homeomorphic to $[-1, 1]^2$. Applying the Tietze Extension Theorem to each coordinate of a continuous map $f : A \to [-1, 1]^2$ gives a continuous extension $F : X \to [-1, 1]^2 \cong D^2$ (B is true). Statement (A) fails for $X = D^2$, $A = S^1$, and $f = \operatorname{id}_{S^1}$ (by the No-Retraction Theorem). Statement (D) fails for $X = [0, 1]$ and $A = \{0, 1\}$ with $f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1$ since $[0, 1]$ is connected.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X = (0, 1) \cup (2, 3) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ with the usual subspace topology. The one-point compactification $X^+$ of $X$ is homeomorphic to:
optionsEn: the disjoint union of two circles $S^1 \sqcup S^1$
the figure-eight space (wedge sum $S^1 \vee S^1$ of two circles joined at a single point)
questions.explanationEn: Adjoining a single point $\infty$ to $(0, 1) \cup (2, 3)$ brings both ends of $(0, 1)$ and both ends of $(2, 3)$ together at $\infty$. Each open interval together with $\infty$ forms a circle $S^1$, and the two circles intersect solely at $\infty$. Thus $X^+$ is homeomorphic to the figure-eight space $S^1 \vee S^1$.

questions.questionTextEn: Let $X = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} X_n$, where each $X_n = \{0, 1\}$ has the discrete topology. Equip $X$ with the product topology $\tau_p$ and separately with the box topology $\tau_b$. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
optionsEn: $(X, \tau_p)$ is compact and discrete; $(X, \tau_b)$ is compact and discrete
$(X, \tau_p)$ is compact and metrizable; $(X, \tau_b)$ is discrete and not compact
questions.explanationEn: By Tychonoff's theorem, $(X, \tau_p)$ is compact, and as a countable product of metric spaces it is metrizable (in fact homeomorphic to the Cantor set). In the box topology $\tau_b$, every singleton $\{(x_n)\} = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \{x_n\}$ is open, so $(X, \tau_b)$ is an uncountable discrete space and hence not compact.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following product spaces (equipped with the product topology) are compact?
optionsEn: $\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} [0, 1/n]$, where each $[0, 1/n]$ has the usual topology
$\prod_{\alpha \in \mathbb{R}} S^1$, where $S^1$ is the unit circle
$\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} [0, n]$, where each $[0, n]$ has the usual topology
$\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} (0, 1)$, where each $(0, 1)$ has the usual topology
questions.explanationEn: By Tychonoff's theorem, an arbitrary product of nonempty topological spaces is compact in the product topology if and only if every factor space is compact. In (A), $[0, 1/n]$ is compact; in (B), $S^1$ is compact; in (C), each $[0, n]$ is compact (boundedness across different factors is irrelevant in the product topology!). In (D), $(0, 1)$ is not compact, so the product is not compact.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following separation properties are preserved under taking ARBITRARY products (with the product topology)?
questions.explanationEn: $T_1$, Hausdorff ($T_2$), and Regular ($T_3$) are all productive (preserved under arbitrary products in the product topology). Normality ($T_4$) is NOT preserved even under finite products: the Sorgenfrey line $\mathbb{R}_l$ is normal, yet $\mathbb{R}_l \times \mathbb{R}_l$ is not normal.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^2$ (with the usual topology) are path-connected?
optionsEn: $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus C$, where $C$ is any countable subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$
questions.explanationEn: (A) Through any two points $p, q \in \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus C$, uncountably many lines pass through $p$ and uncountably many through $q$; pick one line through $p$ avoiding $C$ and one non-parallel line through $q$ avoiding $C$ to obtain a two-segment path in $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus C$. (B) Any two points in the exterior of the open unit disk can be joined by radial and circular arcs. (C) Two parabolas meeting at $(0, 0)$ form a union of two path-connected sets with nonempty intersection, hence path-connected. (D) Removing two points from $S^1$ splits it into two disjoint open arcs, which is disconnected.

questions.questionTextEn: How many distinct $T_0$ topologies can be defined on a 3-element set $X = \{a, b, c\}$?
questions.explanationEn: $T_0$ topologies on a finite set $X$ are in bijection with partial orders on $X$. On a 3-element set, the partial orders are: antichain/discrete ($1$), one comparable pair ($6$), chains of length 3 ($6$), V-posets with one minimal and two maximal elements ($3$), and inverted-V posets with two minimal and one maximal element ($3$). Total = $1 + 6 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 19$.

questions.questionTextEn: How many distinct topologies can be defined on a 3-element set $X = \{a, b, c\}$?
questions.explanationEn: Counting topologies on a 3-element set by their isomorphism classes (up to permutation of $\{a, b, c\}$): indiscrete ($1$), one proper open set of size $1$ ($3$), one of size $2$ ($3$), chains of length $3$ like $\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{a,b\}, X\}$ ($6$), $\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b,c\}, X\}$ ($3$), $\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}, X\}$ ($3$), $\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{a,b\}, \{a,c\}, X\}$ ($3$), $\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}, \{a,c\}, X\}$ ($6$), and discrete ($1$). Summing gives $1 + 3 + 3 + 6 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 6 + 1 = 29$.
